what: Motor A drives an 8-tooth gear that turns a 24-tooth gear, a 3:1 reduction, and the 24-tooth gear turns an 8 mm crank. The crank works a LEGO pneumatic pump, whose piston moves 16 mm per stroke. The pump feeds an air tank that starts precharged to 150 kPa above atmospheric pressure. The program turns the motor nine times forward (three crank turns), pauses, then nine times back to exactly its starting angle. In the simulator the pressure rises from 150.0 to 162.9 kPa, about 2.1 kPa per pump stroke, and stays there although the motor ends where it started.
try: Load the model, press Reset, then Run. Watch the air pressure display and the pump piston.
Count the pump strokes during the forward part: three crank turns give three strokes, and the pressure goes up by about 2 kPa each time.
Watch the reverse part. The crank turns backwards, but the piston still goes in and out, and the pressure keeps rising. Turning back does not suck the air out again.
Use the manual jog on port A in 180° steps. Each 1080° of motor turn is one crank turn and one pump stroke. Watch on which part of the turn the pressure goes up.
Load 'Air Budget — two tanks' and run the same program. The same six strokes raise the pressure by only about half as much.
why: Each inward stroke pushes the air in the pump cylinder through a one-way valve into the tank. On the way back the valve closes, and fresh air flows into the pump from outside. Whichever way the crank turns, every turn makes one inward stroke, so reversing the motor still pumps. One stroke sweeps a volume of A·S = π·(4 mm)²·16 mm ≈ 0.80 cm³ of outside air. Squeezed into the tank's volume V, that adds Δp = p_atm·A·S / V to its pressure (Boyle's law, at constant temperature). The simulator gives the tank and its hoses V = 38 cm³, so each stroke adds 101.3 kPa · 0.80 cm³ / 38 cm³ ≈ 2.14 kPa. Six strokes add 12.9 kPa, as measured.
matters: Every bicycle pump, compressor and tyre inflator works like this: a piston, two one-way valves and a tank. The motor's position says nothing about what is stored: a machine can return to its starting position while energy or material has been moved. In a real pump, some air always stays behind in the cylinder at the end of the stroke. As the tank pressure rises, that leftover air expands again on the return stroke, so each stroke delivers less. The simulator ignores this, so its pressure keeps rising by the same amount every stroke.
question: The motor ends at exactly the angle it started from. Why is the tank pressure higher at the end, and by how much would one more stroke raise it?
answer: Every crank turn, forwards or backwards, makes one inward stroke, and the one-way valve keeps the air it delivers in the tank. Net motor angle does not matter, only the number of inward strokes. One more stroke adds about 101.3 kPa · 0.80 cm³ / 38 cm³ ≈ 2.1 kPa.
further: How many strokes would it take to raise the tank from 150 kPa to 250 kPa, the point where the simulated pump stops charging?
With the two-tank model (75 cm³), predict the rise for six strokes before you run it, then compare.
Suppose a real pump left 0.2 cm³ of air in the cylinder after each stroke. Estimate how much less air it delivers when the tank is at 150 kPa above atmospheric pressure.
formula: Δp per stroke = p_atm·A·S / V; A = π·(4 mm)² = 50.3 mm², S = 16 mm, V = 38 cm³, p_atm = 101.3 kPa → Δp ≈ 2.14 kPa. Gear reduction 24:8 = 3:1, so 1080° of motor A = one crank turn = one stroke.
